name: Thomas S. Kuhn
worldviewSummary: Kuhn argues that mature sciences operate within paradigms — shared exemplars, methods and assumptions — that guide 'normal science' as puzzle-solving. Accumulating anomalies can trigger crises and scientific revolutions, and choosing between paradigms is not settled by a neutral algorithm.
biography: American physicist turned historian and philosopher of science. The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962) became one of the most cited academic books of the twentieth century; Kuhn later refined and qualified several of its claims.

concepts.description: Accepted examples of scientific practice that provide models from which coherent traditions of research spring.
Research firmly based on past achievements, consisting largely of puzzle-solving within the paradigm rather than testing it.
Competing paradigms may differ in standards, problems and meanings of terms, so they cannot be fully compared point by point.

positions.statement: Science does not progress by simple accumulation; revolutions involve a shift in worldview, with scientists after a revolution in some sense working in a different world.
Paradigm choice involves shared values such as accuracy, scope and simplicity, but these do not determine a unique choice; persuasion and community judgement play roles.
Textbooks present science as a linear accumulation and erase the history of revolutions, which shapes how new scientists understand their field.

relations.note: Disagreed with Popper about the role of falsification in actual scientific practice.
